findings.phase_name: OWASP A07 - Identification and Authentication Failures
findings.title: JWT expiration validation disabled
findings.description: JwtVerifier::verify sets validation.validate_exp = false, so issued JWTs are accepted forever regardless of their exp claim.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker who obtains any leaked or old JWT (from logs, browser cache, partner breach, etc.) can authenticate indefinitely. There is no token rotation or revocation, so the only way to stop abuse is to rotate the global JWT_SECRET.
findings.impact: Stolen tokens remain valid forever, leading to persistent unauthorized access including admin operations if the token has role=admin.
findings.recommendation: Remove validation.validate_exp = false and enforce a reasonable exp claim (e.g. 15 minutes for access tokens). Add refresh-token flow in user-service if long-lived sessions are needed.
findings.playbook: Rotate JWT_SECRET immediately, investigate token exposure window, and verify no abused sessions in downstream service logs.

findings.phase_name: OWASP A07 - Identification and Authentication Failures
findings.title: Default JWT secret fallback
findings.description: JWT_SECRET defaults to the literal string 'dev-secret' when the environment variable is not set.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the operator forgets to set JWT_SECRET in production, an attacker can sign a valid JWT with HMAC key 'dev-secret' and role 'admin', then call protected admin endpoints such as /admin/flags/.../enable.
findings.impact: Complete authentication bypass and privilege escalation to admin.
findings.recommendation: Make JWT_SECRET mandatory: panic or fail startup if it is missing. Remove any default secret from source code.
findings.playbook: Audit all running environments for JWT_SECRET value; rotate if it equals 'dev-secret' or any other hardcoded default.

findings.title: CORS allow-origin hardcoded to wildcard
findings.description: CORS_ALLOWED_ORIGINS is parsed in config.rs but never used. The CorsLayer in main.rs always calls allow_origin(Any), emitting Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.
findings.exploit_scenario: Any malicious website can make cross-origin requests to public endpoints such as / (GraphiQL), /query and /ws. While JWT is currently in Authorization header, future cookie-based auth or credentials=true would allow silent authenticated requests from attacker-controlled origins.
findings.impact: Expanded attack surface for cross-origin abuse; security config is silently ignored.
findings.recommendation: Wire cfg.cors_allowed_origins into CorsLayer. Reject the request or omit CORS headers when Origin is not in the allowlist.

findings.title: Unpinned third-party GitHub Action
findings.description: dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable is referenced by a floating tag, not a SHA. The same job later uses secrets.CODECOV_TOKEN.
findings.exploit_scenario: If the dtolnay/rust-toolchain repository is compromised or the @stable tag is repointed to malicious code, the CI runner executes attacker-controlled code with access to repository secrets and can exfiltrate CODECOV_TOKEN or tamper with coverage artifacts.
findings.impact: Supply-chain compromise of CI pipeline leading to secret exfiltration or build tampering.
findings.recommendation: Pin dtolnay/rust-toolchain to a specific SHA and let Dependabot/Renovate update it with review.

findings.title: GraphiQL playground always enabled
findings.description: The root route / unconditionally serves GraphiQL and the schema is built with default introspection enabled. There is no environment toggle.
findings.exploit_scenario: An attacker can visit the public root endpoint to discover the full GraphQL schema, query/mutation names, and field types. This lowers the cost of crafting further attacks (e.g. finding admin-only mutations or id-based access-control gaps).
findings.impact: Information disclosure about API surface and internal data model.
findings.recommendation: Disable GraphiQL and introspection in production builds using an env flag (e.g. ENABLE_INTROSPECTION). The .env.example already defines this flag but the code ignores it.

findings.title: Dockerfile downloads buf without checksum verification
findings.description: The builder stage downloads buf v1.47.0 via curl and installs it without verifying a SHA256 checksum, GPG signature, or cosign attestation.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised GitHub release, supply-chain substitution, or TLS failure could deliver a malicious buf binary. Since buf is executed during build.rs to export and compile proto files, it can alter generated Rust code and therefore the final api-gateway binary.
findings.impact: Build-time supply-chain compromise leading to malicious runtime binary.
findings.recommendation: Verify the published SHA256 checksum of the buf binary after download, or install buf via a package manager with signature verification.

findings.title: Missing CODEOWNERS on workflow files
findings.description: The repository does not have a CODEOWNERS file, so CI workflow changes are not protected by mandatory reviewer approval.
findings.exploit_scenario: A compromised account with write access can modify .github/workflows/ci.yml to exfiltrate secrets, run arbitrary code on pull_request events, or add unpinned actions without requiring a code-owner review.
findings.impact: Reduced protection against malicious or accidental CI pipeline changes.
findings.recommendation: Create CODEOWNERS and assign .github/workflows to a security-sensitive team or maintainer.

findings.title: Unmaintained dependencies proc-macro-error2 and rustls-pemfile
findings.description: cargo audit reports two unmaintained crates: proc-macro-error2 (via validator_derive) and rustls-pemfile (via tonic). No exploitable CVEs were flagged at audit time.
findings.exploit_scenario: Unmaintained dependencies receive no security fixes. A future vulnerability in one of these crates would not be patched promptly and could affect JWT parsing, TLS certificate handling, or validation macros.
findings.impact: Latent supply-chain risk; no immediate exploit path but increases future vulnerability window.
findings.recommendation: Monitor RustSec advisories, pin transitive versions where possible, and evaluate replacements (e.g. updating validator or tonic when patched releases are available).
